abstract: Neuropathic pain is a chronic, debilitating condition characterized by persistent sensory hypersensitivity and frequently associated with anxiety- and depression. Although microglial P2X4 receptors are well-established mediators of early neuropathic pain, their cell-specific contributions to pain maintenance and associated affective disturbances remains poorly understood. We investigated these contributions in male and female mice 30 and 60 days after spared nerve injury (SNI) using conditional P2X4 deletion in microglia (Cx3cr1CreERT2) or neurons (Synapsin-1-Cre), behavioral assessments, and in vivo recordings of spinal dorsal horn wide dynamic range neurons. Microglial P2X4 deletion before SNI completely prevented mechanical allodynia whereas deletion initiated 40 days after injury fully reversed established allodynia in both sexes. Notably, P2X4 immunoreactivity was undetectable in spinal microglia at the late time points examined, suggesting that the sustained contribution of microglial P2X4 may involve mechanisms outside the spinal microglial compartment. Neuronal P2X4 deletion partially attenuated mechanical hypersensitivity and reduced dorsal horn neurons hyperexcitability at day 60 after SNI, supporting a modulatory role in persistent spinal sensitization. Global P2X4 deletion prevented anxiety- and depressive-like behaviors that emerged by day 30 in males and day 60 in females. Whether this protection reflects a direct contribution of P2X4 to affective disturbances or an indirect consequence of reduced pain remains unresolved. Together, these findings identify distinct microglial and neuronal P2X4 contributions to established neuropathic pain and reveal sex-dependent differences in the onset of associated affective disturbances.
